pos: adv. (with sharp grief; rendering Hebrew mar, Greek pikros)
etymology: From bitter, Old English biter, sharp to the taste. Bitterness moves from the tongue to the heart in every language, and Scripture uses both.
biblical_def: Bitterly means with sharp grief. Peter's repentance is recorded in one word: “he went out, and wept bitterly” (Mat 26:75). Isaiah says of the day of the LORD, “the mighty man shall cry there bitterly” (Zep 1:14). The angel of the LORD curses Meroz “bitterly… because they came not to the help of the LORD” (Jdg 5:23), and Naomi says, “call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me” (Rut 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bitterly as with a bitter taste; in a severe manner; sharply; severely; and in a manner expressing poignant grief.
webster_full: BITTERLY, adv. With a bitter taste.
2. In a severe manner; in a manner expressing poignant grief.
3. Sharply; severely; angrily.
scriptures: And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly.
Rut 1:20
And she said unto them, Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. Naomi: that is, Pleasant Mara: that is, Bitter
Jdg 5:23
Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
Zep 1:14
The great day of the LORD is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly, even the voice of the day of the LORD: the mighty man shall cry there bitterly.
corruption_summary: Grief is expected to be expressed in acceptable tones, and Scripture records Naomi renaming herself Bitter and does not correct her.
corruption_paragraphs: Ruth 1:20 is remarkable for what the narrative does not do. Naomi says, call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty. No narrator steps in to soften it, no character rebukes her theology, and the book proceeds to answer her by events rather than by argument. Four chapters later the women tell her the LORD has not left her without a kinsman.

Matthew 26:75 uses the adverb for the turning point of a life: and he went out, and wept bitterly. Two men failed Christ that week. One went out and wept bitterly; the other went out and hanged himself. The difference between Peter and Judas is not the size of the sin but where the grief went, and the Gospels give Peter's grief exactly one adverb and no explanation.
roots_summary: Hebrew mar (H4751), bitter; marar (H4843), to be bitter — the root of Mara and of the bitter herbs of Passover; Greek pikros (G4089), bitter.
roots_lines: Hebrew mar (H4751) — bitter; Ruth 1:20, Exodus 12:8, the bitter herbs.
Hebrew marar (H4843) — to make bitter; Exodus 1:14, they made their lives bitter with hard bondage.
Greek pikros (G4089) — bitterly; Matthew 26:75, Luke 22:62.
usage: “He went out, and wept bitterly” — one adverb, and no explanation.
“Call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me” — uncorrected by the narrator.
“Curse ye Meroz… bitterly” — for staying home from the battle.

etymology: From black, Old English blaec. In Scripture blackness names both a sky in mourning and the reserved gloom of judgment.
biblical_def: Blackness is darkness. Hebrews describes Sinai as what believers have not come to: “ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest” (Heb 12:18). Jude says of false teachers, “to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever” (Jud 13). Isaiah says God clothes the heavens with blackness (Isa 50:3), and Joel describes the day of the LORD as a day of clouds and thick darkness (Joe 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blackness as the quality of being black; black color; darkness; and atrociousness or enormity in wickedness.
webster_full: BLACKNESS, n. The quality of being black; black color; darkness; atrociousness or enormity in wickedness.
scriptures: For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest,
Jud 13
Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.
Isa 50:3
I clothe the heavens with blackness, and I make sackcloth their covering.
Joe 2:2

A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations.
corruption_summary: Believers approach God with the fear appropriate to Sinai, and Hebrews says explicitly that is the mountain they have not come to.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:18-24 is built on a contrast most Christians never hear. Ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest… But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God… and to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant. The terror of Sinai was real, and it is named precisely so the reader will know which mountain he is standing on.

The passage does not remove fear altogether — it ends with our God is a consuming fire — but it relocates it. A believer's reverence is the reverence of someone inside the city rather than someone at the foot of a smoking mountain begging that the word not be spoken to him any more. Confusing the two produces a Christianity that is technically orthodox and functionally terrified.
roots_summary: Hebrew qadruth (H6940), darkness, blackness; Greek gnophos (G1105), gloom; zophos (G2217), the blackness of darkness in Jude 13.
roots_lines: Greek gnophos (G1105) — blackness, gloom; only Hebrews 12:18.
Greek zophos (G2217) — blackness, thick darkness; Jude 6, 13, 2 Peter 2:4, 17.
Hebrew qadruth (H6940) — darkness; only Isaiah 50:3.
usage: “Ye are not come… unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest” — the mountain named to be excluded.
“The blackness of darkness for ever” — Jude's sentence on false teachers.
“I clothe the heavens with blackness” — the sky in mourning.

pos: v. (to redden with shame; rendering Hebrew kalam)
etymology: Middle English blusshen, to glow. A blush is shame made visible — and Scripture notes its absence as a sign of hardening.
biblical_def: To blush is to redden with shame. Jeremiah names its loss as a symptom: “Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush” (Jer 6:15; 8:12). Ezra prays, “O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God” (Ezr 9:6). Zephaniah says of the unjust city, “the unjust knoweth no shame” (Zep 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blush as to redden in the cheeks or face; to be suddenly suffused with a red color in the cheeks or face, from a sense of guilt, shame, confusion, modesty, diffidence or surprise.
webster_full: BLUSH, v.i. To redden in the cheeks or face; to be suddenly suffused with a red color in the cheeks or face, from a sense of guilt, shame, confusion, modesty, diffidence or surprise.
2. To bear a blooming red color, or any soft bright color.
scriptures: Jer 6:15

Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time that I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the LORD.
Ezr 9:6
And said, O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens.
Jer 8:12

Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore shall they fall among them that fall: in the time of their visitation they shall be cast down, saith the LORD.
Zep 3:5
The just LORD is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not; but the unjust knoweth no shame.
corruption_summary: Shamelessness is celebrated as freedom, and Jeremiah lists the inability to blush among the final symptoms before judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 6:15 traces a progression that ends in a physical incapacity: were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush. Note could. The capacity itself had gone. A conscience can be overridden many times, and eventually stops producing the signal, and the prophet treats that silence as the point past which judgment follows — therefore they shall fall among them that fall.

Ezra 9:6 shows the opposite condition in a man who had personally done nothing wrong: O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head. He identifies himself with a sin he did not commit, using the first person plural throughout. Intercession of that kind requires an intact capacity for shame, which is why its loss is so serious for a nation.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalam (H3637), to be humiliated, ashamed, to blush; bosh (H954), to be ashamed.
roots_lines: Hebrew kalam (H3637) — to be ashamed, blush; Jeremiah 6:15, 8:12, Ezra 9:6.
Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, confounded; Jeremiah 6:15, they were not at all ashamed.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — abomination; what they had committed without shame.
usage: “Neither could they blush” — the capacity itself gone.
“I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face” — Ezra over other men's sin.
“The unjust knoweth no shame” — Zephaniah's parallel.

pos: adj., adv. (pertaining to the body; in bodily form; rendering Greek somatikos)
etymology: From body. The word carries the whole weight of the incarnation in Colossians and of a sane view of exercise in Timothy.
biblical_def: Bodily pertains to the body. Colossians states the incarnation with it: “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9). Luke says the Spirit descended on Christ “in a bodily shape like a dove” (Luk 3:22). Paul tells Timothy that “bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things” (1Ti 4:8), and admits his critics said his “bodily presence is weak” (2Co 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bodily as having a body or material form; corporeal; relating to the body, in opposition to the mind; and actual, real.
webster_full: BODILY, a. Having a body or material form; corporeal; as a bodily substance.
2. Relating or pertaining to the body, in distinction from the mind; as bodily defects; bodily pain.
3. Real; actual.
BODILY, adv. Corporeally; united with a body or matter.
scriptures: Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Luk 3:22
And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.
corruption_summary: The body is either idolized or dismissed as irrelevant, and Colossians makes it the place where the fulness of God chose to dwell.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:9 is the New Testament's most compressed statement of the incarnation: for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Not a portion, not an influence, and not temporarily — the word is present tense, written after the ascension. Whatever Christ is now, He is still bodily, which settles a great deal about how Christians should regard matter, resurrection, and their own flesh.

1 Timothy 4:8 is regularly misquoted in both directions: bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things. Paul does not say it profits nothing; he says its profit is small by comparison, having just used athletic imagery approvingly elsewhere. The verse is a ranking, not a dismissal, and the ranking is made by comparing a benefit confined to this life with one that carries promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
roots_summary: Greek somatikos (G4985), bodily, corporeal; soma (G4983), body; pleroma (G4138), fulness — the fulness of the Godhead.
roots_lines: Greek somatikos (G4985) — bodily; Colossians 2:9, Luke 3:22, 1 Timothy 4:8.
Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness; Colossians 1:19, 2:9.
Greek theotes (G2320) — Godhead, deity; only Colossians 2:9.
usage: “In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” — present tense, after the ascension.
“Bodily exercise profiteth little” — a ranking, not a dismissal.
“In a bodily shape like a dove” — the Spirit's visible descent.

etymology: Old English brad. Breadth in Scripture is sometimes mercy's dimension and sometimes the road's fatal advantage.
biblical_def: Broad means wide. Christ warns, “wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat” (Mat 7:13). He condemns those who “make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5). Yet the psalmist praises a different breadth: “thy commandment is exceeding broad” (Psa 119:96), and Job says God would have removed him “into a broad place, where there is no straitness” (Job 36:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines broad as wide; extended in breadth, or from side to side; large; extensive; and open, clear.
webster_full: BROAD, a. Wide; extended in breadth, or from side to side, as distinguished from long, or extended from end to end.
2. Wide; extensive; vast; as the broad expanse of ocean.
3. Large; liberal; as broad views of policy.
4. Open; clear; not covered, confined or concealed; as broad daylight.
scriptures: Mat 7:13
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Mat 23:5
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments,
I have seen an end of all perfection: but thy commandment is exceeding broad.
Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness.
corruption_summary: Breadth is treated as evidence of rightness, and Christ says the broad way is identified precisely by how many are on it.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:13-14 makes crowd size a warning rather than a recommendation: wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it. The road is not broad because it is generous; it is broad because it demands nothing and therefore accommodates everyone. Popularity is offered here as a diagnostic, and it points the wrong way.

Psalm 119:96 shows breadth used positively and unexpectedly: I have seen an end of all perfection: but thy commandment is exceeding broad. Everything the psalmist has examined has a limit he eventually reached; the commandment does not. What looks narrow from outside turns out to have no floor and no far wall — which is why a lifetime in Scripture never exhausts it.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachab (H7342), broad, wide; merchab (H4800), a broad place; Greek euruchoros (G2149), spacious, broad.
roots_lines: Greek euruchoros (G2149) — broad, spacious; only Matthew 7:13.
Hebrew rachab (H7342) — broad, wide; Psalm 119:96, Nehemiah 3:8.
Hebrew merchab (H4800) — broad place, largeness; Job 36:16, Psalm 18:19, he brought me forth into a large place.
usage: “Broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction” — crowd size as a diagnostic.
“They make broad their phylacteries” — religion enlarged for viewing.
“Thy commandment is exceeding broad” — the one thing with no far wall.

pos: adj. (like a beast, senseless; rendering Hebrew baar)
etymology: From brute, Latin brutus, dull. Brutish in Scripture means without understanding — a man functioning below his own nature.
biblical_def: Brutish means senseless as a beast. Asaph confesses it of himself: “So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee” (Psa 73:22). Proverbs says, “he that hateth reproof is brutish” (Pro 12:1). Jeremiah applies it to leaders: “the pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the LORD: therefore they shall not prosper” (Jer 10:21), and says every man is brutish in his knowledge when confronted with idols (Jer 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brutish as pertaining to or resembling a brute or beast; savage; ferocious; gross; carnal; bestial; ignorant; stupid; unfeeling.
webster_full: BRUTISH, a. Pertaining to or resembling a brute or beast; savage; ferocious; gross; carnal; bestial.
2. Ignorant; untaught; stupid; as brutish men.
3. Insensible; unfeeling.
scriptures: So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.
Pro 12:1
Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
For the pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the LORD: therefore they shall not prosper, and all their flocks shall be scattered.
Every man is brutish in his knowledge: every founder is confounded by the graven image: for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them.
corruption_summary: Refusing correction is defended as strength of conviction, and Proverbs classifies it with a single word — brutish.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 12:1 makes an unusually blunt equation: whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish. There is no middle category. A man's response to correction places him on one side or the other, and the word chosen for the wrong side is the word for an animal — a creature that cannot reason about its own behaviour and must be managed by force.

Psalm 73:22 is the more useful verse because it is a confession rather than an accusation. Asaph, having envied the wicked and nearly slipped, looks back and says: so foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee. And then, without a pause: nevertheless I am continually with thee. He calls himself brutish and states God's constancy in the same breath, which is what honest self-knowledge sounds like when it is not despair.
roots_summary: Hebrew baar (H1198), brutish, stupid; from a root meaning to graze or consume — a man reduced to appetite; behemah (H929), beast.
roots_lines: Hebrew baar (H1198) — brutish, senseless; Psalm 73:22, 92:6, Proverbs 12:1, 30:2.
Hebrew behemah (H929) — beast, cattle; Psalm 73:22, I was as a beast before thee.
Hebrew roeh (H7462) — shepherd, pastor; Jeremiah 10:21, the pastors are become brutish.
usage: “He that hateth reproof is brutish” — no middle category offered.
“I was as a beast before thee” — a confession, not an accusation.
“The pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the LORD” — the cause named.

pos: v. (to break open suddenly; rendering Hebrew parats, Greek rhegnumi)
etymology: Old English berstan. To burst is to fail under internal pressure — and Scripture uses it of barns, bottles, and a betrayer.
biblical_def: To burst is to break open. Proverbs promises that honouring the LORD with firstfruits means “so shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine” (Pro 3:10). Christ says new wine must not go into old bottles, “else the new wine doth burst the bottles” (Mar 2:22). Elihu says he is like wine which hath no vent and is “ready to burst like new bottles” (Job 32:19), and Acts records Judas' end (Act 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines burst as to fly or break open with force, or with sudden violence; to suffer a violent disruption; and to break away, to spring from.
webster_full: BURST, v.i. To fly or break open with force, or with sudden violence; to suffer a violent disruption.
2. To break away; to spring from; as, to burst from the arms.
3. To come or fall upon suddenly or with violence; to rush upon unexpectedly.
scriptures: Pro 3:10
So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.
Mar 2:22
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles.
Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles.
Luk 5:37
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles; else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled, and the bottles shall perish.
corruption_summary: New work is forced into old structures because the structures are familiar, and Christ says the result destroys both the wine and the skins.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 2:22 states the consequence twice over: no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles. Both are lost — not only the container. Christ is defending His disciples' failure to fast like the Pharisees, and the argument is structural: something genuinely new had arrived, and forcing it into the old forms would waste it and wreck them.

Proverbs 3:10 uses bursting as blessing rather than failure: thy presses shall burst out with new wine. The condition in the previous verse is honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase. A press that bursts is overfull — the same physics as the wineskin, producing abundance rather than loss because the vessel was ready for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew parats (H6555), to break out, burst; Greek rhegnumi (G4486), to rend, burst; lasko (G2997), to burst asunder, in Acts 1:18.
roots_lines: Hebrew parats (H6555) — to break out, burst forth; Proverbs 3:10.
Greek rhegnumi (G4486) — to burst, rend; Mark 2:22, Luke 5:37, Matthew 9:17.
Greek askos (G779) — wineskin, bottle; the container in question.
usage: “The new wine doth burst the bottles” — both wine and skins lost.
“New wine must be put into new bottles” — the structural conclusion.
“Thy presses shall burst out with new wine” — the same physics, as blessing.

pos: n., adj. (stillness after storm; rendering Greek galene)
etymology: From Greek kauma, heat of the day — the windless hour. A calm is not merely quiet but the cessation of what was violent.
biblical_def: A calm is stillness. Christ rebukes the wind and says to the sea, “Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm” (Mar 4:39). Jonah's sailors are told to cast him forth “so shall the sea be calm unto you”, and when they do, “the sea ceased from her raging” (Jon 1:11–15). The psalmist says God “maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still” (Psa 107:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines calm as still; quiet; being at rest; undisturbed by passion; not agitated; and as a noun, stillness, tranquillity, quiet, freedom from motion, agitation or disturbance.
webster_full: CALM, a. Still; quiet; being at rest; as the air.
2. Undisturbed by passion; not agitated or excited; quiet; tranquil; as the mind, temper or attention.
CALM, n. Stillness; tranquillity; quiet; freedom from motion, agitation or disturbance.
scriptures: Mar 4:39
And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still.
Jon 1:15
So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging.
Mar 4:41
And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
corruption_summary: Peace is sought as the absence of trouble, and the calm on Galilee arrived inside the storm at the word of a Man who had been asleep in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 4:39-41 gives the sequence and the aftermath: he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm… And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? The storm frightened them; the calm frightened them more. A tempest is explicable; a Man who stops one is not.

Psalm 107:29 gives the same act as ordinary divine practice: he maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still. The psalm's structure is a repeated cycle — men in trouble, men crying to the LORD, men delivered, men told to praise. The calm is not an exception in that psalm; it is the fourth of four examples, and the refrain after each is that men would praise the LORD for his goodness.
roots_summary: Greek galene (G1055), a calm; siopao (G4623), to be still — Christ's word to the sea; Hebrew shathaq (H8367), to be quiet.
roots_lines: Greek galene (G1055) — calm; Mark 4:39, Matthew 8:26, Luke 8:24.
Greek phimoo (G5392) — to muzzle, be still; Mark 4:39, peace, be still.
Hebrew shathaq (H8367) — to be calm, quiet; Psalm 107:30, Jonah 1:11-12.
usage: “There was a great calm” — and they feared exceedingly.
“What manner of man is this?” — the calm raised a harder question than the storm.
“He maketh the storm a calm” — listed as ordinary practice.

pos: v. (to deprive, especially of children; rendering Hebrew shakol)
etymology: From be- and reave, to plunder. To bereave is to have something taken by force rather than lost.
biblical_def: To bereave is to be deprived. Jacob says it twice at the lowest points of his life: “me have ye bereaved of my children: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away” (Gen 42:36), and later, “if I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” (Gen 43:14). Ezekiel speaks of a land that has bereaved its nations (Eze 36:13), and Hosea prays, “give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts” in judgment (Hos 9:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bereave as to deprive; to strip; to make destitute; and it is followed by of, and is used especially of the loss of friends by death.
webster_full: BEREAVE, v.t. To deprive; to strip; to make destitute; with of before the thing taken away.
2. To take away from.
BEREAVEMENT, n. Deprivation, particularly by the loss of a friend by death.
scriptures: And Jacob their father said unto them, Me have ye bereaved of my children: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away: all these things are against me.
And God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may send away your other brother, and Benjamin. If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved.
Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they say unto you, Thou land devourest up men, and hast bereaved thy nations;

And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.
corruption_summary: Grief is expected to reach acceptance, and Jacob's surrender in Genesis 43 is not peace but exhaustion — and God honoured it anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 42:36 is one of the most human sentences in the Bible: all these things are against me. Jacob is wrong about every particular — Joseph is alive and governing Egypt, Simeon is safe, and Benjamin will return — and he could not possibly have known it. Scripture records the despair of a man reading his providence backwards, without correcting him in the moment.

Genesis 43:14 is his eventual surrender, and it is bleak rather than serene: and God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may send away your other brother, and Benjamin. If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved. He invokes God's name and then braces for the worst. That is faith at the end of its resources, and the chapter that follows is the beginning of everything being restored to him.
roots_summary: Hebrew shakol (H7921), to be bereaved of children, to miscarry; the same root used of a land bereaving its inhabitants.
roots_lines: Hebrew shakol (H7921) — to bereave, be childless; Genesis 42:36, 43:14, Ezekiel 36:13-14.
Hebrew El Shaddai — God Almighty; Genesis 43:14, the name Jacob invokes at his lowest.
Hebrew racham (H7356) — mercy, compassion; give you mercy before the man.
usage: “All these things are against me” — wrong about every particular, and recorded uncorrected.
“If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” — faith at the end of its resources.
“God Almighty give you mercy before the man” — the name invoked at the lowest point.

pos: v. (to surround a city with an army; rendering Hebrew tsur)
etymology: From be- and siege, from Latin sedere, to sit. A siege is an army sitting down around a city until it yields.
biblical_def: To besiege is to surround a city militarily. The law regulates it with a striking limit: “When thou shalt besiege a city a long time… thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them… for the tree of the field is man's life” (Deu 20:19). Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem (2Ki 25:1), and Ecclesiastes tells of a little city besieged by a great king and delivered by a poor wise man whom no one afterward remembered (Ecc 9:14–15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines besiege as to lay siege to; to beset with armed forces, for the purpose of compelling to surrender, either by famine or by violent attacks; and to beset, to throng round.
webster_full: BESIEGE, v.t. To lay siege to; to beset with armed forces, for the purpose of compelling to surrender, either by famine or by violent attacks.
2. To beset; to throng round.
scriptures: When thou shalt besiege a city a long time, in making war against it to take it, thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them: for thou mayest eat of them, and thou shalt not cut them down (for the tree of the field is man's life ) to employ them in the siege: for

And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about.
Ecc 9:14
There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it:
Ecc 9:15
Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man.
corruption_summary: Total war is justified by necessity, and the law forbade cutting fruit trees even in a long siege — because the tree of the field is man's life.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 20:19 sets a limit that no ancient army observed: when thou shalt besiege a city a long time… thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them: for thou mayest eat of them, and thou shalt not cut them down (for the tree of the field is man's life) to employ them in the siege. Siege warfare consumed timber, and the law protected the food-bearing trees anyway — on the reasoning that the land would still have to feed people after the war.

Ecclesiastes 9:14-15 tells a story with no names: a little city, few men within it, a great king besieging it — now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man. The Preacher's conclusion is double-edged: wisdom is better than strength, and the poor man's wisdom is despised. Both halves are true, and the city was saved regardless.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsur (H6696), to besiege, bind; matsor (H4692), a siege; ets hassadeh, the tree of the field.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsur (H6696) — to besiege; Deuteronomy 20:19, 2 Kings 25:1, Ecclesiastes 9:14.
Hebrew matsor (H4692) — siege, entrenchment; 2 Kings 25:2, Deuteronomy 20:20.
Hebrew ets hassadeh — the tree of the field; Deuteronomy 20:19, given as the reason.
usage: “Thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof” — a limit inside total war.
“For the tree of the field is man's life” — the reason given.
“No man remembered that same poor man” — the city saved by someone forgotten.

pos: n. (the anniversary of a birth; rendering Greek genesia)
etymology: Birth with day. Scripture mentions only two birthday celebrations, and a man dies at each.
biblical_def: A birthday is the anniversary of a birth. Scripture records two observances, both by pagan rulers and both fatal. Pharaoh's birthday: “he made a feast unto all his servants”, restoring the butler and hanging the baker (Gen 40:20–22). Herod's: “when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced… and pleased Herod”, and John the Baptist was beheaded on an oath (Mat 14:6–10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines birthday as the day in which any person is born; and the same day of the month, in which a person was born, in any future year, the anniversary of one's birth.
webster_full: BIRTHDAY, n. The day in which any person is born.
2. The same day of the month, in which a person was born, in any future year; the anniversary of one's birth.
scriptures: And it came to pass the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, that he made a feast unto all his servants: and he lifted up the head of the chief butler and of the chief baker among his servants.
Mat 14:6
But when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.
Mat 14:9
And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath's sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her.
But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.
corruption_summary: Rash promises made in front of an audience are kept out of pride, and Herod beheaded a prophet rather than look weak in front of dinner guests.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 14:9 names the mechanism precisely: and the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath's sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her. He did not want to do it. He did it because he had said something in front of people and could not bear to be seen retracting. The presence of witnesses converted a foolish promise into a murder, and Herod is described as sorry throughout.

The two birthdays in Scripture are a strange pair. In each a ruler holds a feast, exercises absolute power over a man's life, and someone dies — the baker on a gallows, John in a prison. Neither passage moralizes about birthdays as such. What they hold in common is power in a celebratory mood, which the narrative twice presents as a dangerous combination.
roots_summary: Greek genesia (G1077), birthday celebration; Hebrew yom huledeth, day of being born, in Genesis 40:20.
roots_lines: Greek genesia (G1077) — birthday feast; Matthew 14:6, Mark 6:21.
Hebrew yom huledeth — birthday; Genesis 40:20.
Greek horkos (G3727) — oath; Matthew 14:7, 9, the oath's sake.
usage: “Pharaoh's birthday… he made a feast unto all his servants” — one man restored, one hanged.
“For the oath's sake, and them which sat with him at meat” — witnesses converting folly to murder.
“The king was sorry” — and did it anyway.

pos: n. (a pillow or head-support; rendering Hebrew meraashah)
etymology: Old English bolster, a cushion. The Hebrew is simply the place at the head — and it appears in one of Scripture's tensest scenes.
biblical_def: A bolster is a head-support. David and Abishai enter Saul's camp by night and find him asleep “and his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster” (1Sa 26:7). Abishai asks leave to strike; David refuses and takes “the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster” (1Sa 26:12). Michal earlier put a pillow of goats' hair at David's bolster to deceive Saul's messengers (1Sa 19:13,16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bolster as a long pillow or cushion, used to support the head of persons lying on a bed; and a pad, or quilt, to prevent pressure.
webster_full: BOLSTER, n. A long pillow or cushion, used to support the head of persons lying on a bed; generally laid under the pillows.
2. A pad, or quilt, to prevent pressure, support any part of the body, or make a bandage sit easy upon a wounded part.
scriptures: So David and Abishai came to the people by night: and, behold, Saul lay sleeping within the trench, and his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster: but Abner and the people lay round about him.

So David took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster; and they gat them away, and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked: for they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them.
And Michal took an image, and laid it in the bed, and put a pillow of goats' hair for his bolster, and covered it with a cloth.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?
corruption_summary: Opportunity is treated as permission, and David had a sleeping enemy, a spear within reach, and a friend urging him — and refused.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 26:8-9 is the whole argument in two verses. Abishai said, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day: now therefore let me smite him… And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless? The theological reasoning is precise: providence had supplied the opportunity, and providence supplying an opportunity is not the same as God commanding an act.

David takes the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster as proof he had been there, then shouts across the valley from a safe distance. He wanted Saul to know exactly how close he had come and exactly what he had declined to do. The restraint was not passivity; it was demonstrated, and it was demonstrated to the man who had been hunting him.
roots_summary: Hebrew meraashah (H4763), the place at the head, bolster — from rosh, head.
roots_lines: Hebrew meraashah (H4763) — place at the head, bolster; 1 Samuel 19:13, 16, 26:7, 11-12, 16.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head; the root of the word.
Hebrew mashiach (H4899) — anointed; the LORD's anointed, David's stated reason.
usage: “His spear stuck in the ground at his bolster” — opportunity within reach.
“Who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed?” — opportunity is not permission.
“The spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster” — restraint demonstrated.

pos: v. (to take on loan; rendering Hebrew lavah and shaal)
etymology: Old English borgian, to pledge. To borrow is to take with an obligation attached — and Scripture treats failure to return as wickedness.
biblical_def: To borrow is to take on loan. The psalmist draws a moral line: “The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth” (Psa 37:21). Proverbs states the relation: “the borrower is servant to the lender” (Pro 22:7). The law makes the borrower liable for a beast hurt in his keeping (Exo 22:14), and Elisha's students borrow an axe that is lost and recovered (2Ki 6:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines borrow as to take from another by request and consent, with a view to use the thing taken for a time, and return it, or if the thing is to be consumed, to return an equivalent in kind.
webster_full: BORROW, v.t. To take from another by request and consent, with a view to use the thing taken for a time, and return it, or if the thing is to be consumed or transferred in the use, then to return an equivalent in kind.
2. To take from another for one's own use; to copy or select from the writings of another author.
3. To take or adopt for one's own use, sentiments, principles, doctrines and the like.
scriptures: The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
Pro 22:7
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
And if a man borrow ought of his neighbour, and it be hurt, or die, the owner thereof being not with it, he shall surely make it good.
But as one was felling a beam, the axe head fell into the water: and he cried, and said, Alas, master! for it was borrowed. axe
corruption_summary: Consumer debt is normal and unremarked, and Psalm 37 places failure to repay in the same sentence as the description of a wicked man.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 37:21 sets a contrast that most modern readers find surprisingly harsh: the wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth. The wicked man in this verse is not a violent criminal; he is someone who does not pay back what he took. And the righteous man's counterpart behaviour is not scrupulous repayment but giving — generosity is offered as the opposite of default.

Proverbs 22:7 is descriptive rather than condemnatory: the rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. Scripture nowhere forbids borrowing outright; the law assumes and regulates it. What it never does is treat debt as neutral, because the verse names a real transfer of authority. Anyone deciding whether to borrow is deciding how much of himself to hand over, and the arrangement is honest only if he knows that.
roots_summary: Hebrew lavah (H3867), to borrow or lend; shaal (H7592), to ask, borrow; nashah (H5383), to lend on interest.
roots_lines: Hebrew lavah (H3867) — to borrow, lend; Psalm 37:21, Proverbs 22:7, Deuteronomy 28:12.
Hebrew shaal (H7592) — to ask, request, borrow; Exodus 22:14, 2 Kings 6:5.
Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant; the borrower is servant to the lender.
usage: “The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again” — default named plainly.
“The borrower is servant to the lender” — a real transfer of authority.
“Alas, master! for it was borrowed” — the distress of losing another man's tool.

etymology: Old English beorht. Brightness in Scripture attaches to swords, clouds, and finally to a title Christ gives Himself.
biblical_def: Bright means shining. Christ names Himself with it at the very end of Scripture: “I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). Hebrews says the Son is “the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Heb 1:3). A bright cloud overshadows the mount of transfiguration (Mat 17:5), and Ezekiel sees a brightness about the throne like the appearance of the bow in the cloud (Eze 1:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bright as shining; lucid; luminous; splendid; resplendent; and clear, transparent, as liquors; also, evident, clear, manifest to the mind.
webster_full: BRIGHT, a. Shining; lucid; luminous; splendid; as a bright sun or star; a bright metal.
2. Clear; transparent; as liquors.
3. Evident; clear; manifest to the mind, as light is to the eyes.
4. Resplendent with charms.
scriptures: I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Mat 17:5
While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.
Eze 1:28

As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake.
corruption_summary: Christ is pictured chiefly in humility, and the last self-description in Scripture is the bright and morning star — the light that appears when the night is nearly over.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 22:16 is Christ's own final self-designation: I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. The morning star rises last and is brightest, and it appears when the night is at its longest but nearly done. The title is chosen for a church waiting, and it is followed two verses later by the invitation to whosoever will.

Hebrews 1:3 uses the word for the relation between the Son and the Father: who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person. Brightness here is not reflected light but radiance proceeding from its source — the beam is of one substance with the sun and cannot be separated from it. The whole doctrine of the Son's deity is compressed into a metaphor about light.
roots_summary: Hebrew bahir (H925), bright; nogah (H5051), brightness; Greek lampros (G2986), bright; apaugasma (G541), effulgence, in Hebrews 1:3.
roots_lines: Greek lampros (G2986) — bright, radiant; Revelation 22:16, Acts 10:30.
Greek apaugasma (G541) — brightness, effulgence; only Hebrews 1:3.
Hebrew nogah (H5051) — brightness; Ezekiel 1:28, Isaiah 60:3.
usage: “The bright and morning star” — the last self-description in Scripture.
“The brightness of his glory” — radiance of one substance with its source.
“A bright cloud overshadowed them” — the transfiguration.

pos: v. (to command, to invite; rendering Greek kaleo and keleuo)
etymology: Old English biddan, to ask, and beodan, to command — two verbs that merged. The KJV uses both senses.
biblical_def: To bid is to command or to invite. Peter says, “Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water. And he said, Come” (Mat 14:28–29). The wedding parable turns on the bidden who would not come: “they which were bidden were not worthy” (Mat 22:8). Christ counsels, “when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room” (Luk 14:10), and John forbids bidding God speed to a false teacher (2Jn 10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bid as to ask, to request, to invite; to command, to order or direct; to offer, to propose; and to pronounce or declare.
webster_full: BID, v.t. To ask; to request; to invite.
2. To command; to order or direct.
3. To offer; to propose; as, to bid a price at an auction.
4. To proclaim; to make known by a public voice.
5. To pronounce or declare; as, to bid farewell.
scriptures: And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water.
And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.
Mat 22:8
Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy.

But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
corruption_summary: Faith is described as launching out on one's own conviction, and Peter asked for a command first — bid me come — and only then stepped out.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 14:28 contains the most important two words in the account: bid me. Peter does not step onto the water because he believes he can; he asks for a word, and the word given is Come. What he then had under his feet was not his own confidence but a command. When he saw the wind boisterous and began to sink, the word had not changed; his attention had.

Luke 14:10 gives the seating rule, and its logic is social realism: when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher. Christ is not teaching a technique for being promoted at dinners; verse 11 supplies the principle — whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased. The dinner is an illustration of an arrangement that runs much wider.
roots_summary: Greek kaleo (G2564), to call, invite, bid; keleuo (G2753), to command; epo (G2036), to speak, in Matthew 14:28.
roots_lines: Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, bid; Matthew 22:3-9, Luke 14:8-10.
Greek keleuo (G2753) — to command, bid; Matthew 14:28, 19, Acts 25:6.
Greek chairo (G5463) — to greet; 2 John 10, neither bid him God speed.
usage: “Bid me come unto thee on the water” — a command asked for before a step taken.
“They which were bidden were not worthy” — the invitation refused.
“Go and sit down in the lowest room” — a dinner illustrating a wider arrangement.

pos: v. (to seize with teeth; also to exact usury; rendering Hebrew nashak)
etymology: Old English bitan. The Hebrew nashak means both to bite and to lend on interest — the same word for a serpent's strike and a usurer's terms.
biblical_def: To bite is to seize with teeth. Proverbs says of wine, “at the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder” (Pro 23:32). Paul warns the Galatians, “if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another” (Gal 5:15). The law forbids lending “upon usury” to a brother using this same root (Deu 23:19), and Amos says the serpent shall bite the man who leans on a wall (Amo 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bite as to break or crush with the teeth, as in eating; to pierce, as an insect with its proboscis; to cause to smart; and to cheat, to trick.
webster_full: BITE, v.t. To break or crush with the teeth, as in eating; to pierce with the teeth, as a serpent; to seize with the teeth, as a dog.
2. To pinch or pain, as with cold.
3. To reproach with sarcasm; to treat with severity by words or writing.
4. To cheat; to trick.
scriptures: At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.
Gal 5:15
But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of any thing that is lent upon usury:
Amo 5:19
As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him.
corruption_summary: Conflict among believers is defended as contending for truth, and Paul's word for it is what animals do to each other.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 5:15 chooses a deliberately animal image: if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another. He is writing to a church in a genuine doctrinal crisis — the letter's whole subject is a false gospel — and he still warns them about the manner of the dispute. Being right about justification does not license eating one another, and the warning names the outcome: mutual consumption, with no survivors.

Proverbs 23:32 handles wine with the same honesty about delay: at the last it biteth like a serpent. The preceding verse describes the appeal accurately — when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. Nothing about the early experience warns of the ending. That gap between the look at the start and the bite at the last is precisely what makes the warning necessary.
roots_summary: Hebrew nashak (H5391), to bite; and to lend on usury — the same root; Greek dakno (G1143), to bite.
roots_lines: Hebrew nashak (H5391) — to bite, to lend on interest; Proverbs 23:32, Amos 5:19, Deuteronomy 23:19.
Greek dakno (G1143) — to bite; only Galatians 5:15.
Greek katesthio (G2719) — to devour; the companion verb in Galatians 5:15.
usage: “At the last it biteth like a serpent” — nothing at the start warns of it.
“If ye bite and devour one another” — the manner judged even in a real dispute.
“Take heed that ye be not consumed one of another” — the outcome named.

pos: n. (anxiety; also attentive charge; rendering Greek merimna and epimeleomai)
etymology: Old English caru, sorrow, anxiety. The KJV keeps both senses — care as burden and care as responsible attention.
biblical_def: Care means anxiety and also attentive charge. Peter commands the transfer: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7) — one Greek word for the burden, another for God's attention. Christ names “the cares of this world” among the thorns that choke the word (Mat 13:22). Paul lists as his daily burden “the care of all the churches” (2Co 11:28), and Martha is cumbered about much serving and careful about many things (Luk 10:41).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines care as concern; anxiety; solicitude; noting some degree of pain in the mind, from apprehension of evil; and caution, a looking to, regard, attention, or heed, with a view to safety or protection.
webster_full: CARE, n. Concern; anxiety; solicitude; noting some degree of pain in the mind, from apprehension of evil.
2. Caution; a looking to; regard; attention, or heed, with a view to safety or protection.
3. Charge or oversight, implying concern for safety and prosperity.
4. The object of care, or watchful regard and attention.
scriptures: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.
Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches.
And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things:
corruption_summary: Anxiety is treated as an unavoidable feature of responsibility, and Peter commands it be thrown off — while Paul carries the care of all the churches without contradiction.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Peter 5:7 uses two different Greek words in one sentence, and English hides the distinction: casting all your merimna upon him; for he melei for you. The first is anxious care — a divided, distracted mind. The second is attentive concern. The Christian is told to throw the first at God precisely because God has the second toward him. It is not a command to stop caring; it is a command to stop carrying.

Paul's line in 2 Corinthians 11:28 shows the difference in practice: beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches. He was not anxious about them in Peter's sense — he had just listed shipwrecks and beatings without alarm — but he carried a genuine daily weight of responsibility. Responsibility and anxiety are not the same thing, and confusing them makes either duty impossible or worry inevitable.
roots_summary: Greek merimna (G3308), anxious care; melei (G3199), it is a care to, of God's attention; epimeleomai (G1959), to take care of, as the Samaritan did.
roots_lines: Greek merimna (G3308) — anxiety, care; 1 Peter 5:7, Matthew 13:22, 2 Corinthians 11:28.
Greek melei (G3199) — it matters to, he careth; 1 Peter 5:7, Mark 4:38.
Greek epimeleomai (G1959) — to take care of; Luke 10:34-35, 1 Timothy 3:5.
usage: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” — two different words in one sentence.
“The cares of this world… choke the word” — anxiety as a thorn.
“The care of all the churches” — responsibility carried without anxiety.

etymology: Bond with men. A bondman is a man in bondage — and Israel's whole law of servitude is grounded in a memory of having been one.
biblical_def: Bondmen are slaves. Israel's law is grounded in memory: “thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee: therefore I command thee this thing to day” (Deu 15:15). The sabbath command carries the same reason (Deu 5:15), and the release of a Hebrew servant in the seventh year is legislated on it. Ezra confesses, “we were bondmen; yet our God hath not forsaken us in our bondage” (Ezr 9:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bondman as a man slave, or one bound to service without wages; and in old English law, a villain, or tenant in villenage.
webster_full: BONDMAN, n. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages.
2. In old English law, a villain, or tenant in villenage.
BONDMAID, n. A female slave, or one bound to service without wages.
scriptures: And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee: therefore I command thee this thing to day.
Deu 5:15

And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the LORD thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.
Ezr 9:9

For we were bondmen; yet our God hath not forsaken us in our bondage, but hath extended mercy unto us in the sight of the kings of Persia, to give us a reviving, to set up the house of our God, and to repair the desolations thereof, and to give us a wall in Judah and in Jerusalem. to
But thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence: therefore I command thee to do this thing.
corruption_summary: Generosity is grounded in feeling, and Israel's law grounds it in memory — remember that thou wast a bondman, therefore.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 15:15 supplies a motive structure worth copying: thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee: therefore I command thee this thing to day. The command in question is to send a released servant away liberally furnished from flock, floor, and winepress. The reason is not compassion in the abstract but a specific remembered debt — you were slaves, you were bought out, act accordingly.

The same clause grounds the sabbath in Deuteronomy 5:15 and the gleaning laws in Deuteronomy 24:18. Rest, generosity, and justice toward the stranger all rest on one remembered fact. That is why Israel's feasts were memorial meals: a people who forget they were redeemed become a people who treat others as they were once treated.
roots_summary: Hebrew ebed (H5650), servant, slave — the same word used of Moses as the servant of the LORD; abadim hayinu, we were bondmen.
roots_lines: Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant, bondman; Deuteronomy 15:15, 5:15, Ezra 9:9.
Hebrew padah (H6299) — to redeem, ransom; Deuteronomy 15:15, the LORD thy God redeemed thee.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; the verb the whole motive structure rests on.
usage: “Thou wast a bondman… therefore I command thee this thing” — memory as motive.
“We were bondmen; yet our God hath not forsaken us” — Ezra's confession.
“Remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt” — the sabbath's stated reason.

pos: adj. (sharp to the taste; harsh; rendering Hebrew mar, Greek pikros)
etymology: Old English biter, from bite — that which bites the tongue. Scripture moves the word from taste to circumstance to the heart's condition.
biblical_def: Bitter means sharp to the taste, and by extension harsh. Israel eats the passover with bitter herbs (Exo 12:8), and Egypt made their lives bitter with hard bondage (Exo 1:14). The waters of Marah were bitter until a tree was cast in (Exo 15:23–25). Isaiah pronounces woe on those who “put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter” (Isa 5:20), and Hebrews warns against any “root of bitterness springing up” to trouble and defile many (Heb 12:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bitter as sharp, or biting to the taste; acrid; sharp, cruel, severe; painful to the feelings, calamitous; and mournful, distressing.
webster_full: BITTER, a. Sharp, or biting to the taste; acrid; like wormwood.
2. Sharp; cruel; severe; as bitter enmity.
3. Sharp, as words; reproachful; sarcastic.
4. Sharp to the feelings; painful; afflictive; calamitous.
5. Painful to the mind; calamitous; poignant.

corruption_summary: Bitterness is treated as a private feeling with private consequences, and Hebrews describes it as a root that defiles many.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:15 gives bitterness a botany: looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled. A root is underground, slow, and connected to a system. The verse assumes it is possible for one person's unaddressed grievance to poison a congregation, and it assigns the whole church the work of looking diligently — watching for it in one another before it surfaces.

Exodus 15:23-25 supplies the remedy in a picture. Israel came to Marah and could not drink of the waters, for they were bitter. Moses cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet. The bitterness was not drained off or diluted; something was put into it. Preachers have seen a cross in that tree for two thousand years, and the reading holds: bitter water is sweetened by what is thrown in, not by what is taken out.

usage: “They could not drink of the waters… for they were bitter” — three days from the sea.
“The LORD shewed him a tree” — sweetened by what was cast in.
“Lest any root of bitterness… and thereby many be defiled” — a private feeling with public reach.
